column2: smokeEnv makes subprocesses started by smoke tests skip Bootstrap directly.
Strictly, omission would be harmless: os.Executable() is artex.new in the child, so all derived
paths carry the .new prefix and cannot touch actual update files. Relying on this coincidence is fragile;
an explicit short circuit is clear and avoids a needless filesystem probe in the child.
Action is Bootstrap's instruction to main.
Continue: start the server normally.
Restart: exit immediately with ExitRestart so the supervisor script relaunches the process.
State describes update status at this startup so /api/update/check can accurately tell the frontend
whether the last update succeeded or was rolled back.
Bootstrap runs at the very start of main, before listening on any port or opening a database.
Three cases:
1. Staged artex.new exists -> verify and smoke-test; swap and request restart on success, otherwise discard and keep the old version.
2. Only the marker remains -> swap just completed; count an attempt and roll back after enough consecutive failures.
3. Neither exists -> normal startup.
applyStaged handles a staged binary: swap after successful verification, otherwise discard it.
This is the only update path that overwrites the executable and the final gate: smoke tests catch
corrupt downloads, wrong architectures, and missing dynamic libraries. If an unrunnable binary passes,
the supervisor endlessly relaunches it while Go code never runs, so automatic rollback cannot execute.
Swap succeeded. Keep the marker for the next startup, running the new version, to confirm stability.
confirmOrRollback handles startup after a swap: count attempts and restore the old version above the limit.
The counter increments only after Go code starts, covering executable binaries that crash during initialization
(incompatible configuration, occupied ports, failed DB migrations). Pre-swap smoke tests catch binaries that
cannot execute at all; both checks are needed for complete coverage.
If even rollback fails, stop requesting restarts to avoid an infinite loop. Clear the marker
and start in the current state; if startup fails, users can at least see the reason in logs.
Settle confirms the new version is stable and removes the update marker.
main calls it after a delay once HTTP is listening. The process must survive that interval; otherwise retain the marker,
count attempts at subsequent startups, and eventually roll back.
SettleDelay is the runtime required to consider the new version alive.
verifyStaged checks the staged binary: compare SHA256, then actually launch it once.
smokeTest launches the new binary with -h to confirm it can execute on this system.
This catches truncated downloads, wrong architectures (exec format error), missing dependencies, and similar failures.
swap replaces the current binary with the staged new version.
Unix and Windows both permit renaming a running executable (Windows prohibits deletion and
overwriting, not renaming), so no platform branch or prior self-shutdown is required.
Windows rename cannot replace an existing destination; remove the previous update's .old first.
If swapping fails after moving the current version aside, restore it unchanged or the next startup has no executable.
rollback restores the old version backed up by swap.
Move the unstartable new version to .failed for diagnosis rather than deleting it.
Rollback implements /api/update/rollback: explicitly return to the preceding version.
Only swap files; the supervisor script handles restart (the caller then exits with ExitRestart).
Exchange current and backup so rollback can itself be reversed.
HasBackup reports whether a previous version is available, allowing the frontend to show the rollback button.
allowedHosts restricts domains accessible to the update path. Together with checkRedirect below,
any redirect hop to an unlisted host fails immediately: the first gate against DNS poisoning / MITM
replacing the binary. SHA256SUMS verification is the second gate.
Release contains the GitHub Release fields used here.
Asset is a file attached to a Release.
NewClient constructs an HTTP client restricted to GitHub domains. Empty proxy means direct access.
Deliberately do not reuse the default Transport: updates must enforce TLS and certificate verification,
unaffected by settings such as InsecureSkipVerify elsewhere.
checkURL enforces https and the domain allowlist.
FetchLatest queries the latest stable release.
Unauthenticated GitHub API access is limited to 60 requests per IP per hour, easily reached behind a shared outbound IP.
AssetName returns the release archive name for the current platform, matching build.sh package_binary:
artex-<版本>-<os>-<arch>.zip (the version has no v prefix; naming notation preserved).
FindAsset finds a named asset in a Release.
Package selfupdate implements ARTEX's one-click web update: fetch a new binary from GitHub Release,
verify and stage it, then atomically swap it at the next startup.
Responsibilities (see start.sh / start.bat):
Startup script = simple supervisor loop, deciding whether to relaunch after exit based only on the exit code.
This package = all error-prone logic (download / SHA256 verification / smoke test / swap / failure rollback).
Swapping belongs in Go rather than scripts because checksum verification and smoke tests otherwise need separate
sh and bat implementations (sha256sum / shasum / certutil). This is the least tolerable point for error: installing
an unrunnable binary makes the supervisor relaunch endlessly and requires manual host recovery.
A complete update spans three process startups:
1. Old server receives /api/update/apply -> download and verify -> stage artex.new -> exit 75.
2. Script relaunches old version -> Bootstrap finds artex.new -> verify and smoke-test -> swap -> exit 75.
3. Script relaunches the new version -> Bootstrap counts an attempt -> clear marker after successful startup.
Any failure falls back to the old version: at step 2, failed verification deletes staging and keeps running old code; at step 3,
three consecutive failures before marker removal (startup crashes) automatically restore artex.old.
ExitRestart requests supervisor relaunch (EX_TEMPFAIL). Startup scripts immediately restart on this code,
without crash backoff. 0 means normal user shutdown (leave the loop); all other codes count as crashes.
maxAttempts is the allowed number of post-swap startup attempts. Each new-version startup increments the count;
surviving settleDelay removes the marker. maxAttempts consecutive crashes trigger automatic rollback.
Paths contains all files for an update, consistently located under the **Executable directory**.
Deliberately avoid CWD: service working directories may be / or any other path; staging there would
break the swap logic.
ResolvePaths derives all update paths from the current executable.
On Windows, .new/.old must retain the .exe suffix or smoke tests and post-swap execution fail;
strip the suffix before constructing names to keep naming symmetric across platforms.
marker records swap progress to trigger automatic rollback if the new version cannot start.
cleanStaged removes staged files after successful swap, failed verification, or user cancellation, preventing leftover
artex.new from being retried at the next startup.
CompareVersions compares versions, returning -1/0/1 for a<b / a==b / a>b.
ok=false means at least one version is not comparable, such as a local development build "dev" or
git describe output "0.3.7-2-gabc1234-dirty". Callers should disable one-click update in that case,
or a development build could be overwritten by a stable release, losing uncommitted changes.
parseVersion parses "v0.3.7" / "0.3.7" into [3]int.
Accept only clean three-component versions: build.sh uses git describe for untagged builds,
producing suffixed versions such as "0.3.7-2-gabc1234". These must be noncomparable, not interpreted as
0.3.7, or development builds could be incorrectly considered current or overwritten by stable releases.
InDocker reports whether the process runs in a container. A Docker swap writes the container's writable layer;
`docker compose up -d` recreating the container restores the image version. This is expected
(the user is pulling a new image then), but the frontend must explain it clearly.
sumsAsset is the checksum manifest generated by release.yml, covering all Release zip files.
maxBinarySize bounds extracted binary size to prevent malformed zip files from filling the disk.
Phase is an update stage, used directly as the SSE event phase field.
Progress is supplied by callers to push progress to the frontend. pct is meaningful only during download (0-100);
other stages pass -1.
Stage downloads the current-platform archive from the specified Release, verifies it, and stages the binary as artex.new.
Use the full zip, not a bare binary, for two reasons: existing Release SHA256SUMS already
cover only zip files, avoiding CI changes and supporting historical releases; archives also contain
skills/, leaving room for future built-in skill synchronization. The only cost is a few hundred extra KB.
Returning means staging is complete; callers then shut down gracefully and exit with ExitRestart.
Place all temporary files in the destination directory so the final rename is atomic within the same filesystem
(cross-device rename fails, and /tmp is often a separate mount).
Store the staged binary's sha256 separately for rechecking before the next startup's swap,
protecting against changes or corruption between staging and restart.
The marker affects only automatic rollback; the staged file is ready, so marker failure does not interrupt updating.
fetchSums downloads and parses SHA256SUMS, returning filename -> hexadecimal digest.
parseSums parses a sha256sum-style manifest, returning filename -> hexadecimal digest.
Accept an entry only when the first field is 64 hexadecimal digits. Checking only for two fields is insufficient:
any two-word explanatory line would become an entry, inserting garbage in the checksum table,
potentially matching a real asset with an incorrect digest.
Format: "<sha256>  <filename>" (sha256sum uses two spaces; shasum binary
mode prefixes filenames with *).
download writes an asset to dst while computing SHA256 and reporting progress from Content-Length.
get performs an allowlisted GET and returns the response body.
extractBinary extracts the artex executable from the release archive.
Archive layout is artex-<版本>-<os>-<arch>/artex, but match by **basename**, not a constructed full
path: the version already appears in the archive name, and a single naming typo breaks updating; basename matching tolerates changes.
checkWritable checks directory writability early. Otherwise non-root operation or binaries in system
directories would fail only at swap time after downloading tens of MB.
progressWriter counts written bytes and rate-limits reports, avoiding an SSE event for every 32KiB chunk.
Even when the archive path has no historical host directories (new installs store traffic only in SQLite + _blobs),
it must retain a journal. If a crash occurs between PostgreSQL and SQLite commits, restart
rolls back the SQLite transaction; only the journal lets recovery complete host-row deletion. Without it,
traffic exclusively owned by cold-tier tasks would remain in the hot database forever.
Reduce to a minimal index: retain only locator fields plus response code/length, never response content.
